doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Piano licks, writing for soloists and a tribute to Curtis Peagler
summary: Jeannie and Jimmy explain how they write arrangements around each soloist's pet phrases and how they honored Curtis Peagler with 'Mr. CP'.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well let me talk about your music for a bit. You have certain piano licks I think you like a lot.
Yes.
[scats] I mean I hear that, right?
Yes.
As soon as I hear that, I mean it sets up so much. It sets up the tempo—
It does.
It sets up a nice groove.
That’s true.

And it’s a sound that I will associate with you. And when you come up with — I mean you seem to have quite a bag of licks. Are these things, when you sit to write an arrangement, are they things that you hear in your head beforehand? Or do you need to hear the tune first? How do you decide exactly what to write behind a certain song? Is that something you can answer?

Well actually, fundamentally, I’m a firm believer in going into the aspect of the intuitive side for utmost, as far as the intellectual part, I mean given the scientific lean and the voice of notes and things like that. Because even intuitively, I get sounds that I hear, and when I hear it then I go—
And it depends on who’s solo. See if we know it’s Snooky, then he knows certain things that help support what Snooky does. Right?

Yeah and then writing, like when we do the group sounds and things like that, and Jeannie’s background, when we’re playing for Jeannie, there’s a certain nuance that happens, in terms of everybody. So that we just get that wonderful, how can I say it, homogeneous —
That’s a good word.
Feeling. And out of it comes the sound.
And sometimes we tease them you know. Sometimes we make a riff, it’s one of the soloist’s favorite things that they play, and we’ll put it in the riff. Then they’ll say—
No that was the intent.
We’ll put it in the riff then they’ll start to do it, and it’s there, so then—
Now they’ve got to go somewhere else.
Hey, you know, Ellington used to do that all the time too, right? I like that thing, I think I’ll write a tune around it.

He was a main thief boy. You could hear him, when the guys would take a solo, and he’d be playing, then answer, and go hmmm. And you could tell, he really liked it because all in and out he’d be playing it all along.
To be sure to don’t forget it.
He could have gone broke if he had to pay royalties to all the fellows that he took licks from.
Snooky had certain things, Curtis Peagler had his certain thing, and naturally Cat Daddy and Ricky Woodard, he had his certain thing. You’d always know it’s Ricky because you hear this thing.
Yeah. Once you hear it, oh, that’s Ricky.

That’s their schtick. Everybody has their stamp of what — like Sweets you know. [scats] And Curtis always did that. [scats] And so on the last record, “The Good News Blues,” we did Mr. CP and we dedicated it to him. So we took all of his pet phrases and put it together on that song. It’s on the record we gave you.
Cool.
And on the soloing part.
We took his whole solo [scats].
And we saved it.
That was just like Curtis.
And it was really funny watching him run into it.
I played that?
Because since he died, you know, really, everybody misses him. Because he could really set a fire.
And in all sincerity, the two of us, and also a couple of the other guys, they feel, every time Curtis makes his presence on that bandstand.
Yeah. Because I’ll never forget—
They’ll mention it.
